questions.q: Do all liquids conduct electricity?
questions.a: No - pure water barely conducts; liquids with dissolved acids, bases or salts conduct well.

questions.q: Name two conducting and one non-conducting liquid.
questions.a: Conducting: salt water, lemon juice. Non-conducting: distilled water (or pure oil).

questions.q: How can you test whether a liquid conducts?
questions.a: Set up a circuit with the liquid, two electrodes, a bulb or LED; glowing shows conduction.

concepts.title: LED as a Weak Current Detector

questions.q: Why is an LED used instead of a bulb in conduction tests?
questions.a: A bulb glows only with strong currents; an LED lights up with weak currents many liquids allow.

questions.q: How many leads does an LED have and how is it connected?
questions.a: Two - the longer (positive) lead joins the battery's positive side; reverse and it stays dark.

questions.q: What does a dim glow in the LED tell us?
questions.a: The liquid conducts, but weakly - it is a poor conductor compared with metals.

questions.q: How can magnetism show that a current flows in a liquid?
questions.a: Place a compass near the circuit - current's magnetic effect deflects the needle even when the current is weak.

questions.q: What happens to a compass needle when current stops in the tester?
questions.a: It swings back to its normal north-south direction.

questions.q: Why does the deflection show conduction?
questions.a: Only a current in the liquid can create the magnetic effect that moves the needle.

questions.q: Why is pure water a poor conductor but tap water a good one?
questions.a: Dissolved salts of tap (and drinking) water carry ions; pure water has almost none.

questions.q: What makes sea water the best conductor among natural waters?
questions.a: It holds the most dissolved salts, so many free ions carry current.

questions.q: Should we touch a switch with wet hands? Why?
questions.a: No - water with dissolved salts on skin conducts current and can give a shock.

questions.q: What are the chemical effects of electric current?
questions.a: Current passing through a conducting liquid causes bubbles of gas, metal deposits or colour changes.

questions.q: Give one example of a chemical effect of current.
questions.a: Passing current through acidified water splits it into hydrogen and oxygen (electrolysis).

questions.q: What happens when current passes through copper sulphate solution with carbon electrodes?
questions.a: Copper moves to one electrode; gas bubbles appear at the other - a chemical change occurs.

questions.q: What happens during electrolysis of water?
questions.a: Water splits into hydrogen and oxygen gases, appearing as bubbles at the two electrodes.

questions.q: Which gas forms in greater amount at the electrodes of water electrolysis?
questions.a: Hydrogen, double the volume of oxygen (water is H2O).

questions.q: Why is a little acid added to water before electrolysis?
questions.a: Pure water hardly conducts; the acid supplies ions that let current flow.

questions.q: Electroplating deposits silver at 0.01 g per second. How much silver deposits in 5 minutes?
questions.a: 3 g

questions.q: A chromium bath lays down 0.002 g of metal each second. Find the deposit in 10 minutes.
Copper deposits at 0.005 g/s. What mass coats an object in 4 minutes?
Gold plating adds 0.0005 g per second. How much gold is laid on in 2 minutes?
A nickel bath deposits 0.008 g each second. Compute the coating on a spoon left 6 minutes.
Name two uses of electroplating.
questions.a: Chromium plating of car parts and taps for shine and rust-proofing; tin plating of cans to keep food safe.

questions.q: Why is cheaper jewellery electroplated with gold or silver?
questions.a: A thin coat of the costly metal gives the look at a fraction of the price.

questions.q: How does electroplating protect iron objects?
questions.a: A coat of zinc or chromium keeps air and moisture away, stopping rust.

questions.q: An ORS packet says 4 spoons of powder in 200 mL of water. Find the strength and spoons needed for 100 mL.
questions.a: 2 spoons

questions.q: A gardener mixes 3 spoons of fertiliser in 600 mL of water. What is the strength per mL, and spoons for 100 mL?
questions.a: 0.5 spoons

questions.q: 2 spoons of sugar dissolve in 500 mL of solution. Find the concentration and the spoons for 100 mL.
questions.a: 0.4 spoons

questions.q: A disinfectant needs 5 spoons in 250 mL. Calculate its strength and spoons for 100 mL.
questions.a: 2 spoons

questions.q: A drink mix uses 1 spoon in 50 mL. What is the strength, and how many spoons for 100 mL?
questions.a: 2 spoons
